prompt: Classify each database operation as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE.

items.snippet: Get all users whose account was created after Jan 1, 2025
items.explanation: Retrieving existing data is always SELECT — it reads rows without changing them. You'd write: SELECT * FROM users WHERE created_at > '2025-01-01';

items.snippet: A user submits a sign-up form and a new account is created
items.explanation: Adding a new row to a table is INSERT. The form data maps to column values: INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES ('Rivka', 'rivka@example.com');

items.snippet: A user changes their email address in account settings
items.explanation: Modifying an existing row is UPDATE. Always use a WHERE clause: UPDATE users SET email = 'new@example.com' WHERE id = 42; — without WHERE, every row would be changed.

items.snippet: An admin removes a banned account from the system
items.explanation: Removing rows is DELETE. Be careful with WHERE: DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 99; removes one row; DELETE FROM users; (no WHERE) removes all of them.

items.snippet: Display the five most recent orders placed on the site
items.explanation: Fetching data to display is SELECT. You'd add ORDER BY and LIMIT: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;

items.snippet: A product goes out of stock — mark its quantity as 0
items.explanation: Changing a value in an existing row is UPDATE: UPDATE products SET quantity = 0 WHERE id = 12; The row still exists — you're just changing one of its values.
